name: Ben Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm Ben, I'm 43. I did twenty years in the army, joined at seventeen, and when I came out I went labouring. Now I'm a junior formwork carpenter, about two years in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Formwork is the timber and ply moulds you build so they can pour concrete into them, walls, columns, floor slabs. We're on a seven-storey office block right now. I'm in at six, toolbox talk at quarter past, then it's building shutters, propping, stripping them down after the pour and cleaning them for the next lift. I like the routine and the lads, it's the nearest thing to a section in the army. What wears me out is the reading of drawings, I was never one for paper, and the foreman, Dave, has to explain things to me more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you are, told you so. Lot of fuss about computers that turned out to be a better spellcheck. I'd say it at the canteen and leave it there, I'm not on social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing, which is how I like it. I've got my army pension coming in, Karen's childminding, and a trade I'm getting better at. A computer can't carry a sheet of ply up a ladder in the rain, and I never thought it could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, learn the job, get my ticket next year. Church on Sunday, coach Josh's football team on Saturday morning. Keep paying the mortgage like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Life as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Never have. The kids use it for homework and I tell them it's cheating. Karen says I'm behind the times, and she's probably right, but I don't trust a thing I can't see working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the army you learn not to trust what you can't check. If a bloke tells you the bridge is safe, you go and look at the bridge. These computers tell you things with total confidence and half the time they're making it up, from what the kids say.

S0.say: I'd say I told people so, and that AI turned out to be a better spellcheck. I'd say it in the canteen and leave it there, since I'm not on social media.
S0.think: He thinks it means nothing changes, which he likes, with his army pension, Karen's childminding and a trade he's getting better at.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, learning formwork and aims for his ticket next year. Keeps up church, coaching his son's football team and normal mortgage payments.
S0.quote: A computer can't carry a sheet of ply up a ladder in the rain, and I never thought it could.
S0.fieldNote: Ben's twenty years in the army shape his distrust of anything he can't check for himself. He never uses AI and calls it cheating when his kids do. His army pension gives him a quiet sense of security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will adjust, they always do, and it's up to each man to get on with it. I wouldn't want the government throwing money at it. Apprenticeships, yes, handouts, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd not be too bothered. Formwork is heavy, messy, every pour is different, and the sites are muddy. I've seen what a laptop does when you drop it in a puddle, so I'm not worried about one running a concrete pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and keep learning. If the company brought in some new machine and said learn it, I'd learn it, slowly. I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated at all the talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'up to each man to get on with it'. What about people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then their family and their church should help them, like ours did when my dad got hurt. That's what community is. I don't mind the government helping a bit, but it shouldn't be the first place you go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on site you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Liam, he's nineteen and only does this because his dad pushed him. He's not interested, he's on his phone at every break. Funny enough, if the machines come, he's the one who'd be fine, because he likes all that.

S1.say: I'd say people will adjust and it's up to each person to get on with it. Apprenticeships yes, handouts no, and no government throwing money at it.
S1.think: He wouldn't be too bothered, because formwork is heavy, messy and different every pour, and muddy sites are no place for laptops.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and keeps learning formwork. Learns any new machine the company brings in, slowly, but doesn't seek it out.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little irritated by all the talk.
S1.quote: I've seen what a laptop does when you drop it in a puddle, so I'm not worried about one running a concrete pour.
S1.fieldNote: Ben's traditional view puts family and church before government when people struggle, based on his own family's experience. He doubts tech can survive a muddy site. He notes, with some humour, that the young lad he worries about would cope best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and someone should have thought before letting a few tech firms change everything overnight. I'd say men need work, not cheques. I'd say that to anyone at church or the club who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried, but not for the money so much. The pension pays the basics and we've savings. It's not the wage I'd miss. It's having somewhere to be at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back where we could, the new van, the holiday. Pay more off the mortgage while I still had wages. Talk to the pastor and my brothers about what we do as a family, and keep turning up at work until they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not like panic, the army trains that out of you, but a heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working. Saving. I'm not going to sit at a computer learning to be something else at 44, I'd be terrible at it. I'd make sure the house was nearly paid and the kids were sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Karen say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we'll manage, and we would, money-wise. But she knows what I was like when I first came out of the army, the year I didn't have a job. I was no good to anyone that year, and she'd be worried about that more than the bills.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness to let a few tech firms change everything overnight, and that people need work, not cheques. I'd say it at church or the club.
S2.think: He'd be worried, but less about money, since the pension covers basics. What he'd miss is having somewhere to be at six in the morning.
S2.do: Cuts back on the new van and holiday and pays more off the mortgage while wages last. Talks to his pastor and brothers about the family's plans and keeps working until told to stop.
S2.feel: Anxious, a heavy feeling rather than panic.
S2.quote: It's not the wage I'd miss. It's having somewhere to be at six in the morning.
S2.fieldNote: For Ben, AGI threatens purpose more than income, since his army pension covers the basics. The year without a job after leaving the army clearly still hurts. He'd lean on church and family, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to sort themselves out if they're willing to work. I'd say the young ones should get trades the machines can't do yet. I'd not be ranting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps me. I'd be 48, the mortgage would be close to done, and with the pension I could live quietly. I'd have five more years of being a carpenter, which is three more than the fast one, and I'd take every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving, make sure I've my ticket. I'd wait and see what the company did before doing anything daft. Maybe put a bit by for Josh to start a trade when he leaves school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It would sit in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with the lads, mainly, and getting the house paid off. I don't need to become anything new, I just need to finish what I've started. Three years is three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Some people would use five years to retrain. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did my retraining when I came out of the army, and it took me two years to be half decent. I'm not built for starting over every five minutes. Some men are, good luck to them.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people willing to work to sort themselves out, and young people should get trades machines can't do yet.
S3.think: He thinks five years helps: the mortgage close to done and the pension enough to live quietly. He'd take every extra year of being a carpenter.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving and gets his ticket, waiting to see what the company does before changing anything. Puts a bit aside for Josh to start a trade after school.
S3.feel: Uneasy, sitting at the back of his mind.
S3.quote: I'd have five more years of being a carpenter, which is three more than the fast one, and I'd take every one of them.
S3.fieldNote: For Ben the extra years are about finishing what he started and time with the lads. He's firm that he isn't built for starting over again. He still pictures his son going into a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody has an excuse. Families should plan, firms should take on apprentices while they can, and people should stand on their own feet. I'd not want a big government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is my whole working life left, near enough. I'd be 53, I'd have the house paid and the pension, and I'd probably stop when the robots come anyway. I'd spend ten years getting good at something, then hand it to a machine and go fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I am: work, learn, save. I'd talk to Josh and Ellie about what they want to do and push them towards something with people. I'd keep coaching the football and going to church, that doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for the kids than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push them towards something with people. Not a trade like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard bit. I always thought I'd tell Josh to get a trade, like a proper man. Telling my son not to learn a trade would feel like telling him not to go to church. But if the robots are doing it by 2036, maybe nursing, maybe teaching, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not blame exactly. The people building it think they're doing good, I suppose. I'd just say they've forgotten that work isn't only about money, it's what makes a man get out of bed.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and nobody has an excuse: families should plan, firms should take on apprentices and people should stand on their own feet, without a big government scheme.
S4.think: He sees ten years as nearly all of his working life left; with the house paid and the pension, he'd probably stop when robots arrive and go fishing.
S4.do: Keeps working, learning and saving as now. Talks to Josh and Ellie about their futures and pushes them towards jobs with people, while keeping up football coaching and church.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for the kids than for himself.
S4.quote: Telling my son not to learn a trade would feel like telling him not to go to church.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years almost fits Ben's remaining working life, so his worry turns to his children. Advising his son against a trade clashes deeply with his values. He doesn't blame the AI builders but thinks they've forgotten what work means.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for the money, for what I'd do with my days. What would help is apprenticeships and real work, even if it's fixing things the robots break, not a cheque in the post. And the church and the community pulling together, like they did for my dad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the army. I've seen men come out with nothing to do and fall apart. If this happens to millions at once, that's what I'd worry about, not the bills.

headlineQuote: I'd spend ten years getting good at something, then hand it to a machine and go fishing.
portrait: Ben Olsen is a 43-year-old junior formwork carpenter on an office block, who served twenty years in the army before labouring and then learning the trade. His army pension and savings mean money isn't his main fear; losing a reason to get up at six is. He's traditional, churchgoing and distrustful of AI, which he never uses, and he prefers family and community help to government cheques. He's calm about the plateau and steady change, anxious about AGI in two years, and uneasy with more time, when his worry shifts to his children's futures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for the money but for losing what to do with his days.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and real work, even fixing what robots break, instead of cheques, plus church and community pulling together.
